summary: Extends Kerberos so a client can talk to a service without revealing its identity, or revealing only its realm, and can obtain anonymous credentials from the key distribution center. It updates RFC 4120, RFC 4121 and RFC 4556. Its status is historic and it was replaced by RFC 8062.

eli5.summary: Like buying a ticket without giving your name. This lets a person prove they may enter without saying who they are.

questions: can i use kerberos without revealing my identity
subtitle: Proving your credentials without revealing who you are.

tldr.problem: Kerberos normally requires a client to reveal its identity to the Key Distribution Center (KDC) and then to application servers. Some applications need to authenticate a service and secure communications without disclosing the client's identity for privacy reasons.
tldr.mechanism: The specification extends Kerberos to allow clients to request anonymous tickets by setting a new anonymous KDC option, and defines anonymous PKINIT for completely anonymous authentication without revealing identity even to the KDC. Clients can use these anonymous tickets to prove they are authorized without revealing who they are.
tldr.outcome: The Kerberos anonymity extensions enable privacy-preserving authentication but have been superseded by later specifications as Kerberos continues to evolve.

today: RFC 6112 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 8062 as Kerberos continues to evolve with improved anonymous authentication capabilities and clearer specifications for deployment.

sections.title: Anonymous Authentication in Kerberos
sections.content:
Kerberos is a network authentication system where a client proves its identity to a service using tickets issued by a Key Distribution Center (KDC). Normally, both the KDC and the service learn the client's identity. However, some applications need clients to authenticate services for trust (ensuring the service is genuine) while protecting client privacy.

This specification defines two ways to achieve this: first, a client can authenticate to the KDC normally using its identity but request an anonymous ticket, revealing its identity only to the KDC; second, anonymous PKINIT allows a client to request an anonymous ticket without revealing its identity to the KDC at all, using only public-key cryptography. In both cases, the client receives a ticket marked as anonymous that can be used with any application server without revealing the client's identity.
sections.eli5: Normally, to use a service through Kerberos, you tell the key distribution center 'I am Alice, give me a ticket' and then you use that ticket with the service. With anonymity, you can say 'give me a ticket but do not put my name in it' or 'give me a ticket and I will not even tell you who I am'.

sections.title: Anonymous Principals and Tickets
sections.content:
The specification defines two new concepts: the anonymous principal (WELLKNOWN:ANONYMOUS) is a well-known identity that represents an anonymous user, and the anonymous realm (WELLKNOWN:ANONYMOUS) indicates that a ticket was issued anonymously.

An anonymous ticket is a Kerberos ticket with specific properties: it contains the anonymous principal as its client name, it contains no information that reveals the client's identity (though it may contain information about the client's realm or group membership), and it has the anonymous ticket flag set. The ticket may be marked with either the client's real realm (if the client authenticated with its identity) or the anonymous realm (if using anonymous PKINIT).

A new anonymous KDC option is defined that clients set in requests to indicate they want an anonymous ticket instead of a normal one.
sections.eli5: An anonymous ticket is a special certificate that says 'this person is allowed to use this service' but does not say who the person is. It is marked with a special flag so the service knows it is an anonymous ticket.

sections.title: Getting Anonymous Tickets from the KDC
sections.content:
A client requests an anonymous ticket by setting the anonymous KDC option in an AS (Authentication Service) request. The client can authenticate using its normal credentials (password or certificate) and ask for an anonymous ticket, in which case its identity is known to the KDC. The KDC then issues a ticket containing the anonymous principal name instead of the client's name.

Alternatively, the client can use anonymous PKINIT to avoid revealing its identity even to the KDC. The client sends a special PKINIT (Public Key Initial Authentication) request without signing it or providing a certificate, using only Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The KDC validates the Diffie-Hellman parameters but skips the usual checks that would verify the client's certificate and identity. The resulting ticket is marked with the anonymous realm, confirming that the KDC never learned the client's identity.
sections.eli5: To get an anonymous ticket, you either tell the KDC 'I am Alice but give me an anonymous ticket' (and then the KDC knows you are Alice, just not the service), or you do anonymous PKINIT where you just prove you can do the math without saying who you are (and nobody except you knows).

sections.title: Using Anonymous Tickets
sections.content:
Once a client has an anonymous ticket, it can use it in TGS (Ticket Granting Service) requests to obtain service tickets, or directly with an application server. When using an anonymous ticket in a TGS request, the client sets the anonymous KDC option again, and the KDC will issue a new anonymous ticket for the service being requested.

The client realm in these subsequent exchanges depends on how the original anonymous ticket was obtained. If obtained with the client's identity known to the KDC, the realm is the client's real realm. If obtained via anonymous PKINIT, the realm is the anonymous realm. This lets the service distinguish between 'anonymous person from my realm' and 'completely anonymous person'.

Application servers that receive an anonymous ticket can verify its validity and know that the client is authorized to use the service, but they cannot determine who the client is beyond what the ticket reveals (which may be realm membership or group membership from authorization data).
sections.eli5: You use the anonymous ticket like any other Kerberos ticket: the service checks it is valid and that you are allowed to use the service. The service knows you are authorized but not who you are.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The anonymity feature is effective only if the underlying cryptography is sound and if the KDC and client properly handle the anonymous principal and realm names. Authorization data in anonymous tickets must be carefully reviewed to ensure they do not leak information about the client's identity. For example, authorization data showing the client belongs to a specific group of users can reveal membership even if the individual is not named.

The combination of Kerberos authentication with anonymity lets a client prove it is authorized without revealing identity, but the service still knows the client came from a particular realm (or is completely anonymous). If absolute client anonymity is required even at the realm level, anonymous PKINIT should be used.
sections.eli5: Anonymous tickets work only if everyone honestly follows the rules and does not accidentally put your name in the authorization data. The realm being revealed tells the service where you come from, even if not exactly who you are.
